findings.quote: This paper shows that a learned component model acquires all of these properties from where its approximation is placed and how its condensed stiffness is formed
findings.problem: The properties just listed include being 'improvable at deployment without retraining'. That property does not come from where the approximation is placed or how Ŝ is formed. It comes from a third element, the correction W, and holds only when the smoothing interval contains the spectrum (4.3; checked per geometry in 5.2). As written, the thesis sentence claims improvability with no hypothesis and credits it to the wrong element.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence "This paper shows that a learned component model acquires all of these properties from where its approximation is placed and how its condensed stiffness is formed, and quantifies what then determines its error in the assembled compliance and in the local thickness sensitivity." with: "This paper shows that a learned component model acquires the structure of a mechanical model from where its approximation is placed and how its condensed stiffness is formed, and its improvability from a fixed correction of its interior field. It also quantifies what then determines the error in the assembled compliance and in the local thickness sensitivity."
notes: defender(refuted): The current thesis sentence matches the paper's own framing. In this paper the correction is part of how the condensed stiffness is formed: Ŝ = FᵀKF with F = WÊ. The correction also acts in the interior extension, i.e. where the approximation is placed. The abstract says the same thing: it asks for 'controlled and improvable accuracy', answers 'The answer lies in where the approximation is placed and how its condensed stiffness is formed', and then gives the correction 'applied inside that energy' as the third part of that answer. Changing only the Introduction would break this parallel with the abstract. The spectrum-containment hypothesis is already stated two paragraphs later in the same Introduction ('when the smoothing interval contains the spectrum'), and the property preservation holds for any fixed linear W (6.2). The proposed fix also has a dangling 'inside that energy': paragraph 1 never mentions an energy. It would repeat the containment caveat a third time in the front matter, against the brief's caveat policy.

expert(modified): The problem is real. Introduction paragraph 1 says improvability, like the other properties, comes from placement and how the condensed stiffness is formed. The abstract says instead 'Learning supplies the trial field, the variational form the structure, and the correction the improvability', and Conclusions line 543 says the model 'acquires the structure of a mechanical model from where its approximation is placed and how its condensed stiffness is formed', with the correction added separately. The proposed fix has three problems. 'Inside that energy' has no antecedent, because paragraph 1 never mentions the energy form. 'Smoothing interval contains the spectrum' uses terms not yet introduced; that hypothesis is already stated in paragraph 3 and the abstract, and it belongs to 4.3 and 5.2 under the caveat policy. And the fix chains a third 'and' into an already long sentence. Splitting the sentence in two keeps the parallel with the abstract and the Conclusions.

findings.quote: improvable without loss of these properties, assemblable and differentiable, for any symmetric positive semidefinite discrete model
findings.problem: Contribution (i) leaves out two hypotheses. First, the ordering S ⪯ Ŝ_tg ⪯ Ŝ_0 behind 'improvable' requires the smoothing interval to contain the spectrum (and an exact coarse solve, 4.3). Second, the results require A = K_II ≻ 0 and the rigid-body assumption, not just any SPSD model: Section 2 and Section 6.4 both state 'a positive definite interior block'.
findings.fix: Replace contribution (i) with: "(i) A construction principle for learned component models, valid for any discrete model with a symmetric positive semidefinite stiffness and a positive definite interior block: on the complete retained space of a cell, a learned linear interior extension, a fixed geometry-specific two-grid correction and the transpose of the complete extension are combined in one condensed energy, and the resulting condensed stiffness is symmetric and positive semidefinite with the rigid-body kernel, bounded below by the exact Schur complement, assemblable and differentiable, and improvable without loss of these properties by a correction that cannot increase the error when its smoothing interval contains the spectrum."
notes: defender(modified): The scope problem is real. Section 2 ('a symmetric positive semidefinite stiffness whose interior block is positive definite') and Section 6.4 ('a symmetric positive semidefinite stiffness and a positive definite interior block') both require A = K_II ≻ 0. Contribution (i) says only 'any symmetric positive semidefinite discrete model', and without A ≻ 0 neither S nor E exists. The containment insertion is not needed and could mislead. 'Without loss of these properties' holds for any fixed linear correction; 6.2 says 'The variational properties hold for every input, and the ordering for every geometry whose spectrum the smoothing interval contains'. Attaching 'whenever the smoothing interval contains the spectrum' to that phrase suggests the properties depend on containment. The hypothesis is already in the abstract and Introduction paragraph 3. Only the scope is fixed, worded as in 6.4.

expert(modified): The problem is real. 'For any symmetric positive semidefinite discrete model' leaves out A = K_II ≻ 0, which Section 2 (opening and 2.2) and Section 6.4 (line 539) both require; without it S is not even defined. 'Improvable' also lacks the containment hypothesis that the abstract states. The proposed wording 'improvable without loss of these properties whenever the smoothing interval contains the spectrum' wrongly suggests that keeping the properties depends on containment. In fact Ŝ − S = HᵀAH ⪰ 0 holds for any fixed W that preserves retained values; only the ordering S ⪯ Ŝ_tg ⪯ Ŝ_0 needs containment. With the trailing 'for any discrete model …' clause after a long qualifier, its scope is also unclear. Moving the model class to the head of (i) and attaching the hypothesis to the correction fixes both. An exact coarse solve is part of the construction, so it need not be stated here.

findings.quote: an amplification of displacement error into energy error in thin walls
findings.problem: The paper derives ε = δ²κ (Appendix B.3) and measures κ, but never ties large κ to wall thinness: no thicker-wall comparison exists. B.3 explicitly says the analysis does not determine 'a continuum bending-mode label'. The data tie large κ to the cut: κ is 124–7089 in M1, M2, H1 and H2, while the uncut thin-walled U2 has κ = 85 and turns δ = 0.74% into ε = 0.40% (5.4).
findings.fix: Replace contribution (ii) with: "(ii) An error analysis from the component to the structure and to the design: the interior error enters the compliance through a load-specific share-weighted bound and the thickness sensitivity through the stiffness derivative, with a linear term that the energy error does not control, which makes joint accuracy of compliance and local sensitivity the design criterion; and the factorisation \(\varepsilon=\delta^2\kappa\) of the energy error into a relative displacement error and a stiffness ratio shows how interior displacement errors of about one percent become energy errors of 2–35% in the cut cells examined (Section 5.4)."
notes: defender(modified): The attribution to thin walls is unsupported. Section 5.4 never mentions wall thickness, there is no thin-versus-thick comparison, and every cell in the paper is thin-walled. The data separate cut cells from the uncut cell: in the cut cells κ is 124–7089 and ε is 2–35%; in U2 κ is 85 and δ = 0.74% gives ε = 0.40% (evidence/RESULTS_TABLES.md, delta/kappa column). The proposed text is factually wrong, though. It says 'sub-percent displacement errors', but the cut cells have δ = 1.26% (M1), 1.15% (M2), 1.23% (H1) and 0.71% (H2), mostly above one percent. Its 'by which' also makes an identity the cause of the amplification. A minimal locative replacement fixes the problem without adding a new claim to the contribution list. It matches the wording proposed for Section 2 and the Conclusions (findings 3 and 4).

expert(modified): The problem is real. Section 5.4 measures κ and never mentions wall thickness. No thin-versus-thick comparison exists, and every cell is thin-walled, so 'in thin walls' asserts a cause the data cannot isolate. Table ST04 gives base-network κ of 124 (H1), 294 (M2), 866 (M1) and 7089 (H2) in the cut cells, against 85 for the uncut U2. One correction to the finding: B.3 declines the bending label for the cumulative low-mode error energy, not for κ in general; the point still stands. The proposed fix is numerically wrong. It says 'sub-percent displacement errors', but the base-network δ in the cut cells is 0.71–1.26% (Table ST04), i.e. about one percent. Its 'by which …' clause is also followed by the existing 'which makes joint accuracy …', giving two chained relative clauses whose antecedents become unclear. The rewrite below closes the design-criterion argument with a semicolon and states the measured range (2–35%, Section 5.4).

findings.section: 2. Discrete substructures and static condensation (opening paragraph)
findings.quote: and its thin walls amplify interior displacement error into energy error (Section 5.4)
findings.problem: Same causal attribution to thin walls as in the Introduction. Section 5.4 shows the amplification in the cut cells (κ 124–7089) and much less in the uncut thin-walled U2 (κ = 85, ε = 0.40% from δ = 0.74%). Appendix B.3 explicitly declines a mechanical interpretation of κ.
findings.fix: Replace with: "and interior displacement errors of about one percent can become energy errors of several percent in its cut configurations (Section 5.4)".
notes: defender(confirmed): This is an explicit causal claim ('its thin walls amplify'), and the cited Section 5.4 does not support it. 5.4 never mentions wall thickness and reports the large amplification only in the cut cells: δ 0.7–1.3% and κ 124–7089 give ε of 2–35%. The uncut, equally thin-walled U2 has δ = 0.74%, κ = 85 and ε = 0.40%. Nothing in the main text, appendices or supplement links κ to thinness, membrane or bending action, and B.3 avoids a bending-mode reading. The replacement is accurate ('about one percent' covers 0.71–1.26%; 'can become ... several percent' matches the wording of 6.1), keeps the hard-instance argument and fits the sentence grammatically.

expert(confirmed): The problem is real. Section 5.4 attributes the amplification to error lying 'in directions far stiffer, relative to their amplitude, than the exact field', not to wall thickness. Table ST04 shows κ of 124–7089 in the cut cells against 85 in the uncut, also thin-walled U2. The replacement is a descriptive clause that fits the list of reasons the instance is hard, and 'about one percent' matches δ = 0.71–1.26%. The wording 'several percent' matches the Conclusions. Optional smoother wording: '…, and in its cut configurations interior displacement errors of about one percent can become energy errors of several percent (Section 5.4)'.

findings.quote: and in thin walls a displacement error of about one percent lies in stiff directions and becomes an energy error of several percent
findings.problem: The conclusion turns the cut-cell observation of 5.4 into a general statement about thin walls. The only uncut thin-walled cell measured (U2) shows the opposite: δ = 0.74% gives ε = 0.40%, not 'several percent'. No thin-versus-thick comparison exists, and B.3 says κ carries no bending interpretation.
findings.fix: Replace with: "and in the cut cells examined a displacement error of about one percent lies in stiff directions and becomes an energy error of several percent".
notes: defender(confirmed): As a general statement about thin walls, this sentence is contradicted by the paper's own data. The uncut thin-walled U2 has δ = 0.74% and ε = 0.40% (5.4; evidence/RESULTS_TABLES.md: 'U2 ... 0.74%, 85'), not several percent. The 'about one percent becomes several percent' behaviour is shown only for M1, M2, H1 and H2 (δ 0.71–1.26%, κ 124–7089, ε 2–35%), and no thin-versus-thick comparison exists. The fix keeps the sentence structure and the 'stiff directions' point (large κ in the cut cells), and it matches 6.1 and the Section 2 fix.

expert(confirmed): The problem is real. The Conclusions state as a general thin-wall fact what Section 5.4 measured only in cut cells. Table ST04 gives the uncut U2 δ = 0.74% and κ = 85, and Table ST05a gives its mean energy error as 0.402%, not several percent. The replacement 'in the cut cells examined' is minimal, keeps the sentence's structure and the clause 'lies in stiff directions' (correct, since κ = R(d)/R(u) is large), and matches the δ range of 0.71–1.26%.

findings.quote: at the price of tens of thousands of coarse degrees of freedom per cell
findings.problem: In Sections 4.3 and 5.5 and Table 1, 'coarse DOFs' are the unknowns of the Q1(17) coarse-grid correction: 5,601 for the 165,927 interior DOFs of M1, i.e. thousands, not tens of thousands. Here the phrase means the retained DOFs of the assembled model (the 1.7–2.6×10⁴ just stated). Read with the body's meaning, the sentence is wrong by an order of magnitude.
findings.fix: Replace "at the price of tens of thousands of coarse degrees of freedom per cell" with "at the price of an assembled model that carries all of these retained degrees of freedom".
notes: defender(modified): The mismatch is real. In the body, 'coarse DOFs' means the unknowns of the Q1(17) coarse-grid correction: 5,601 for M1 (5.5), 4,557 for M2 and 7,950 for U1 (Table ST08). These are thousands, not tens of thousands, and the clause comes right after 'with the correction', so readers will take it that way. The git history shows the original 'tens of thousands of coarse coordinates per cell' meant the unknowns of the assembled (coarse) model, i.e. the 1.7–2.6×10⁴ retained DOFs. The term-map substitution turned this into a collision with 4.3/5.5. The proposed text uses 'DOFs', but the brief defines that abbreviation at first use in Section 2.2, and the Introduction spells out 'degrees of freedom' everywhere. The fix should spell it out too.

expert(modified): The problem is real. In this paper 'coarse DOFs' are the unknowns of the Q1(17) coarse-grid correction (term map, decision 4; Section 5.5). Table ST07 gives 7,950 (U1), 5,601 (M1) and 4,557 (M2): thousands, not tens of thousands. The phrase was meant in the PIML sense of the preceding sentence ('coarse models'), which clashes with the paper's own term. The proposed fix uses the abbreviation 'DOFs', which is first defined in Section 2.2 and is otherwise absent from the abstract and Introduction (the brief says these spell out 'degrees of freedom'). It also repeats 'per cell' after '1.7–2.6×10^4 degrees of freedom per cell' in the same sentence. The rewrite keeps the intended contrast with the small coarse models of PIML.

findings.quote: it rarely admits assembly, carries no bound, cannot be improved once trained
findings.problem: 'Carries no bound' is stated flatly, but Introduction paragraph 3 itself credits learned shape functions evaluated as NᵀKN (Huang et al. 2023) with the Ritz lower bound by the exact Schur complement. The abstract therefore contradicts the paper's own account of prior work.
findings.fix: Replace "it rarely admits assembly, carries no bound, cannot be improved once trained, and its error in the quantities that analysis and design require is unknown" with "it rarely admits assembly or carries a bound, cannot be improved once trained, and its error in the quantities that analysis and design require is unknown".
notes: defender(modified): There is a minor real inconsistency. Read literally, 'carries no bound' is flat, while Introduction paragraph 3 credits learned shape functions evaluated as NᵀKN (Huang et al. 2023) with the Ritz lower bound. Putting 'rarely' in charge of both items fixes this at no cost. (The R3 readthrough accepted the sentence apart from the change to 'admits assembly', but that is not one of the binding decisions.) The proposed replacement leaves a grammatical flaw, though. The text after the quote continues ', and its error ... is unknown', so the result would be 'or carries a bound, and cannot be improved once trained, and its error ...', a double-'and' chain. The replacement should keep a three-item list.

expert(modified): The problem is real but minor. 'Seldom' hedges the sentence, yet the flat 'carries no bound' conflicts with Introduction paragraph 3, which credits learned shape functions evaluated as N^TKN (Huang et al. 2023) with the Ritz bound. The proposed fix breaks the list. Spliced in, it gives '…or carries a bound, and cannot be improved once trained, and its error … is unknown', with two coordinating 'and's. Keeping the three-item list fixes this.

findings.quote: thickness optimisation reproduces the design of exact condensation to 0.0051 per corner parameter
findings.problem: The twin optimisation with exact condensation was run only for case A, the 2×2×2 block (5.10, Table 6). The plates were checked at selected designs, not reproduced. The abstract reads as a general statement about thickness optimisation.
findings.fix: Replace with: "thickness optimisation of an eight-cell block reproduces the design of exact condensation to 0.0051 per corner parameter".
notes: defender(confirmed): Section 5.10 and Table 6 support the twin optimisation with exact condensation and the 0.0051 bound only for case A, 'the 2×2×2 block of Section 5.8' ('their final corner parameters differ by at most 0.0051'). The plates B1 and B2 were optimised only with NICE and checked against exact condensation at selected designs (Table ST27). The abstract states the result as general. The preceding clause ('An eight-cell design iteration ...') hints at the context but does not limit the claim. 'An eight-cell block' matches 5.8's wording ('a 2×2×2 block of eight distinct cells'), adds four words and changes no number.

expert(confirmed): The problem is real. Section 5.10 and Table 6 show that only case A, the 2×2×2 block with four cut cells, was optimised as a twin with exact condensation: final corner parameters differ by at most 0.0051. Plates B1 and B2 and the X-z run were checked by exact condensation only at selected designs, and Hom-y and X-y are 'Not checked'. The fix names the eight-cell block, which keeps the abstract accurate at minimal cost. 'Eight-cell' also appears earlier in the same sentence, which is acceptable. Optionally, 'the design obtained with exact condensation to within 0.0051 in every corner parameter' (the wording of the Conclusions) is slightly clearer.

findings.quote: the method of moving asymptotes reproduces the design obtained with exact condensation to within 0.0051 in every corner parameter
findings.problem: This is the single case A twin (eight cells, 24 versus 23 iterations), stated without its scope. No exact-condensation twin exists for the plates.
findings.fix: Replace with: "the method of moving asymptotes reproduces on an eight-cell lattice the design obtained with exact condensation to within 0.0051 in every corner parameter".
notes: defender(confirmed): The 0.0051 figure comes from the single case A twin: a 2x2x2 block, NICE in 24 iterations against exact condensation in 23 (Section 5.10, Table 6). No exact-condensation optimisation exists for the plates. In the conclusions the sentence speaks of 'the design' with no scope, so it can be read as a general result. Adding the scope is cheap and correct. It contradicts no decision, and R3 fixed only the wording, not the evidence base. 'Corner parameter' is an allowed term.

expert(modified): The problem is real. The 0.0051 agreement comes from the single case A twin (8 cells; 24 and 23 iterations; Table 6 and the 5.10 text). The plates were only checked design by design against exact condensation and have no twin optimisation. The next clause, 'on cut 24-cell plates', suggests the first result belongs to some other case but never says which. The proposed fix is right in substance, but 'case A' is a Section 5.10 label that the Conclusions never define. A scope that stands on its own reads better, and it matches 'lattices of eight learned cells' earlier in the same paragraph.

findings.quote: whereas a homogenised model underestimates the compliance by 27–37%
findings.problem: The 'whereas' contrast suggests the homogenised model is unfit for this design task, but the body reports something more nuanced. Its designs, evaluated with NICE, lie within 1.1% of B1 and 0.34% below B2; the bending result is confirmed exactly (Table ST27). The continuation from Hom-z ends 0.87% below the NICE design B2 (5.10, ST23c). The 27–37% measures compliance prediction, not design quality, and leaving out the design comparison overstates the advantage.
findings.fix: Replace with: "whereas a homogenised model underestimates the compliance by 27–37%, although its designs, evaluated with NICE, have compliances within 1.1% of those of the NICE designs".
notes: defender(modified): The 27–37% compares compliance prediction with compliance prediction, which is fair. But it sits in a design sentence, and leaving out the design result tempers the contrast. Table 6: Hom-y evaluated with NICE is 88.02 against B1 87.09 (+1.07%); Hom-z is 1,341.8 against B2 1,346.4 (-0.34%). Hom-z is therefore better than B2. The proposed 'come within 1.1% of the NICE designs' reads as if both homogenised designs were slightly worse, so the wording should be neutral. This does not touch decision 6, which only governs the 5.10 prose.

expert(modified): Confirmed against the records. Evaluated with NICE, Hom-y is 1.07% above B1 and Hom-z 0.34% below B2 (S9.3). In the exact model Hom-z is 1,342.30 against 1,346.85 for B2, still 0.34% lower (Table ST27). So a homogenised design is at least as good as the NICE design in bending. The 27–37% is a prediction error, and setting it against NICE with 'whereas' implies a design advantage the body does not show. Adding the design comparison is correct and contradicts no decision; the 'optimisations are local' caveat stays in Table 6 and 6.4. The proposed wording needs two changes. 'come within 1.1% of the NICE designs' does not say which quantity is compared. The Conclusions carry no other cross-references, so '(Section 5.10)' is out of place.

findings.quote: the correction alone reduces the base network's error on the hardest cell by two orders of magnitude without retraining
findings.problem: 'The hardest cell' is defined nowhere. On H2, the cell with the largest base error (35%), the reduction is about 3,000× (to 0.0117%, Table 3). On M1 it is about 70× (13.5% to 0.186%). The population evidence that the main line rests on is not given at all: the mean over 80 geometries falls from 6.89% to 0.0965% (5.3), and all fourteen two-cell configurations fall within both references (5.6).
findings.fix: Replace with: "the correction alone, applied to the base network without retraining, lowers its mean energy error under consistent tractions on the 80 validation geometries from 6.89% to 0.0965% and keeps its compliance and sensitivity errors below 1% in the fourteen two-cell configurations evaluated".
notes: defender(modified): 'The hardest cell' is defined nowhere in the paper; the only other 'hardest' is the main-line phrase about cut cells. The deleted original meant M1 (13.5% to 0.19%, about 73x). Read as H2, which has the largest base error and the heaviest cut, the factor is about 2,990x, so the phrase is ambiguous. The population result is checked: 6.89% to 0.0965% under consistent tractions (5.3, ST03). The corrected base network meets both 3% criteria in all fourteen configurations where it was evaluated (ST09 note; largest sensitivity error 0.945%). The proposed fix leaves out the loading class, and 'both references' is undefined in the conclusions. The reference is defined in 5.1 as 'A 3% line on compliance and on each cell's sensitivity vector'.

expert(modified): The problem is real. 'The hardest cell' is defined nowhere. By base error it is H2, where the reduction is 35/0.0117, about 3,000 times (Table 3). Only M1 (13.5% to 0.186%, about 73 times) matches 'two orders'. Using the population evidence is right and matches decision 1. Two changes to the proposed wording: (a) 6.89% and 0.0965% are means under consistent tractions, and paragraph 3 of the Conclusions states that loading class for 0.074%, so it is stated here too; (b) 'both references' (the 3% lines of 5.1) means nothing in the Conclusions. Table ST09 gives the corrected base network's maxima as 0.079% in compliance and 0.945% in sensitivity, over the fourteen selection-cell configurations, which are the only ones it was evaluated on.

findings.quote: and in every example a better initial field or a larger correction budget reduced the energy error
findings.problem: 'Better initial field' is undefined, and the records contain counterexamples if the harmonic start counts as better than the zero interior. Under nodal forces the zero start ends below the harmonic start on H2 (0.0056% vs 0.0246% at 32 steps per stage; also at 16 and 64 steps) and on U2 (1.19% vs 1.25% at 32 steps) (ST08b). Also, the larger-budget evidence covers only the base network, harmonic and zero starts; NICE itself was never run with a larger budget.
findings.fix: Replace with: "and in every example a larger correction budget reduced the energy error further, whether the correction started from the base network's field or from a deterministic field".
notes: defender(modified): The counterexample is real. In U2 under nodal forces the harmonic start begins better than the zero interior (energy error 1475% against 2743%, evidence/p1_checks_u2.json), yet ends worse after correction: 3.53% against 3.40% at 16 steps per stage and 1.25% against 1.19% at 32 (ST08b). In H2 under nodal forces the harmonic start begins at 1028% against 468,000% for the zero interior (p1_checks_cpu.json), yet ends higher at 16, 32 and 64 steps. So 'a better initial field ... reduced the energy error' is false as written. The budget half holds: every ST08b row and every Figure 8a/d curve decreases. The proposed replacement puts supplementary table citations into the conclusions and repeats the learned-start comparison, which the next sentence already makes ('a deterministic start leaves ... more error than the learned field'). Deleting the false half is enough.

expert(modified): Confirmed in ST08/ST08b. Under nodal forces the zero start ends below the harmonic start, which has the lower error after 8 steps: on H2, 0.134 vs 0.181 (16 steps), 0.0056 vs 0.0246 (32) and 1.09e-4 vs 5.18e-4 (64); on U2, 3.4 vs 3.53 (16) and 1.19 vs 1.25 (32). So 'a better initial field ... reduced the energy error' does not hold. Every ST08b row does decrease with k, which is consistent with 4.3 (an ordering is guaranteed, monotonicity in k is not), so the larger-budget claim stands as an observation. NICE was never run at a larger budget. The proposed wording has three problems: 'harmonic and zero starts' are not defined in the Conclusions; 'the learned start ending lowest' repeats the next sentence ('a deterministic start leaves ... more error than the learned field'); and it cites supplementary tables where the Conclusions cite nothing else.

findings.quote: a deterministic start leaves one to four orders of magnitude more error than the learned field
findings.problem: Table 3 and Section 6.1 give factors of 7 to 290 for the harmonic start and 2,400 to 12,000 for the zero interior. On H2 the harmonic factor is 6.9, below one order of magnitude.
findings.fix: Replace with: "a deterministic start leaves 7 to 12,000 times the error of the learned field".
notes: defender(refuted): Table 3 gives ratios to the base network's corrected field of 6.9 to about 11,900, which is 10^0.84 to 10^4.08. Rounded to whole orders, that is 'one to four orders of magnitude', the usual reading of the phrase. R3 §4 (row '6.1 ↔ 7 ↔ 5.5') explicitly replaced the factors in Section 7 with orders of magnitude, because they are already given in 5.5 and 6.1. The fix would bring back a third repetition that the authority removed. The editor's change from R3's 'one to three' to 'one to four' already corrected the upper end against Table 3.

expert(modified): Confirmed against Table 3. Against the corrected base network, the harmonic start gives factors of 92 (M1), 246 (M2), 98 (H1), 6.9 (H2) and 290 (U2). The zero interior gives 5,900, 11,900, 3,000, 2,400 and 11,100. The range is therefore 6.9 to 12,000: less than one order of magnitude at the low end and just over four at the high end. The 5.5 phrasing 'lower by factors of 7 to 290 ... and 2,400 to 12,000' supports the numeric replacement. In the proposed text, '7 to 12,000 times more error than' is ambiguous: 'n times more' can be read as n+1 times as much. The Table 3 reference is also dropped for consistency, since the Conclusions cite nothing else.

findings.quote: The construction transfers to other component families with new training data
findings.problem: 'Transfers' implies that the method works for other families once retrained, which was not tested. Section 6.4 says other TPMS families were not tested and need new training data and network parameters. Only the structure and the error relations are family-independent.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence "The construction transfers to other component families with new training data; the structure and the error relations do not depend on the family." with: "The construction and the error relations do not depend on the component family; the trained network does, and another family requires new training data."
notes: defender(refuted): R3 §4 prescribed this sentence verbatim, and it agrees with 6.4: 'The construction and the error relations are not specific to the cells studied: they apply to any discrete model with a symmetric positive semidefinite stiffness and a positive definite interior block. The trained network is [specific] ... Other TPMS families were not tested; they ... require new training data and network parameters.' The subject is 'the construction' (the method), not the trained network's accuracy, and 'with new training data' already states the condition. The fix would drop the method's applicability, which 6.4 supports. It would also add a caveat to the conclusions, which R3's caveat policy keeps in 6.4 only.

expert(modified): The problem is real. 'transfers ... with new training data' implies the retrained method works on other families, and that was not tested. Section 6.4 supports only family-independence of 'the construction and the error relations' ('The trained network is [specific]'). However, the proposed fix adds 'and were not tested'. That repeats a 6.4 limitation in the Conclusions, against the caveat policy ('state it there once'; R3: the Conclusions do not repeat caveats). The replacement below removes the overclaim with a factual contrast and repeats no caveat. It keeps 'construction', the term used in 6.4.

findings.quote: the linear term of Eq. (9) contributes only 7.2% and 0.79% of the sum of the linear- and quadratic-term norms, so the quadratic term dominates these finite errors
findings.problem: The main text reports only the two cells where the linear term is negligible, so it reads as evidence against the linear term that contribution (ii), the abstract and the conclusions rely on. Table ST05a shows the term is substantial wherever the error is smaller: 28–43% under consistent tractions in U1, U2 and H1, and up to 72% under nodal forces. This is the regime of the corrected variants, and this supporting result is never announced.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "At fixed retained displacement, M1 has mean energy and field-based sensitivity errors of 13.5% and 14.1%, and H2 of 35% and 75.1%; the linear term of Eq. (9) contributes only 7.2% and 0.79% of the sum of the linear- and quadratic-term norms, so the quadratic term dominates these large errors. The linear term is not negligible elsewhere: it contributes 28–43% under consistent tractions in U1, U2 and H1, whose energy errors are below 2%, and 24–72% under nodal forces in all six cells; being first order in the field error, it dominates as that error tends to zero (Table ST05, Figure S03)."

Reporting only M1 and H2 in the main text undercuts contribution (ii) and the conclusions. Three problems with the proposed append. After '(Table ST05, Figure S03)', 'it' would refer back to 'the quadratic term'. 'In the cells with smaller errors' is too broad: M2 (3.64%) has only 9.3%. The better fix aligns the Introduction with 2.3, item for item and in the same order. Requiring the error to be traceable to the sensitivities already requires that sensitivities be delivered, so Section 2.3 needs no change. The time ratios below therefore compare one GPU with 16 CPU threads." Leave 6.3 and the twin's description in S9.2 unchanged.

The proposed fix, however, goes against an earlier author decision (review_r1/CONSOLIDATED.md I-01, DECIDED): same-GPU exact factorisation timings were deliberately removed from Table 5 and the discussion, and host PARDISO was kept as the baseline because it is conventional practice. findings.section: 5.5 Reducing interior error with fixed network parameters
findings.quote: Two, four and eight steps per stage give 1.02%, 0.422% and 0.186% on M1, and the eight-step cycle about 0.027% on M2 and U1
findings.problem: Table ST08b shows that 16 steps per stage on the base network already beat NICE's 8-step cycle on all five cells of Table 3 (M1 0.12% vs 0.131%, M2 0.0135% vs 0.0358%, H2 0.0016% vs 0.0148%). With 16 steps per stage, the base network beats NICE's 8-step result on all five cells: M1 0.120 vs 0.131, M2 0.0135 vs 0.0358, H1 0.00487 vs 0.0115, H2 0.00163 vs 0.0148, U2 0.00202 vs 0.00465. Under nodal forces M1 is also lower, 0.0695 vs 0.0835. ST07 states that all network rows use the base network, so NICE was evaluated only with its trained cycle. The problem is real. The proposed fix, though, leaves an [x] placeholder for which the paper has no source: the network-versus-correction split of the application time was a placeholder in earlier drafts and was never filled. The comparison is at equal correction, not at equal application time: the cost of one network pass relative to one 8 / \(Q_1(17)\) / 8 cycle is not reported separately, and a harmonic start followed by several cycles was not evaluated."

The 24-cell plate is plate B1, and exact condensation was run on it (Table ST27, start and final designs, with exact PCG iteration counts), so 'neither exact route was run at these sizes' is false. The referee's concern is already answered in the main text: statistics are given for the 60 geometries outside selection (5.3 gives 0.077% against 0.074%, plus the 95th/99th percentiles and maximum; ST03d), and nine cells outside selection are assembled in 5.6 as an independent check.

The main text calls the other 60 geometries 'outside selection', but they are outside parameter selection only, not outside the choice of variant. A referee should be told this in Section 5.1. Two changes to the fix. First, 'these 80 geometries' coming right after 'the 60 geometries' is ambiguous. findings.section: 5.2 Verification of the discrete reference and of the corrected operator
findings.quote: The spectrum containment thus holds on every geometry tested
findings.problem: The ordering guarantee rests on spectrum containment, which was verified only for the 80 validation geometries. The lattice cells and the many regenerated cells of the optimisations use the same 40-step power estimate with a 5% margin. The paper does not say whether containment was checked for them, or what a failure would do.
findings.fix: Replace with: "The spectrum containment thus holds on all 80 validation geometries; it was not checked for the cells of the lattices and optimisations of Sections 5.8–5.10, which use the same 40-step estimate. Where it fails, the smoothing is no longer guaranteed to be nonexpansive and the ordering of Eq. (15) can be lost; symmetry, positive semidefiniteness and \(\widehat S\succeq S\) do not depend on it."
notes: defender(refuted): The current wording is the one the R3 readthrough prescribes, item 1.2(b): "so the spectrum containment holds on every geometry tested; symmetry, positive semidefiniteness and Ŝ ⪰ S do not depend on it." The scope is clear because the same sentence says the endpoint was checked "on all 80 validation geometries". The caveat table puts the per-geometry containment caveat in 5.2, and 6.2 already states the conditional ("the ordering for every geometry whose spectrum the smoothing interval contains (Section 5.2)"). What happens on failure is already in Appendix D ("eigenvalues above b can be amplified"; the ordering of Eq. (15) needs ρ_k<1). The proposed text also contains an unresolved placeholder ("[checked on … / not checked]"), so it cannot be applied as written.

expert(modified): The problem is real. The Lanczos check (evidence/lam_check_val80.json, Appendix D) covers only the 80 validation geometries. The sixteen lattice cells of Section 5.8 were generated for those examples and are not among the 80, and the optimisation cells are regenerated at every design iteration. No endpoint check of either set exists in the evidence or in S9, and the review files R4/CONSOLIDATED say the check was offline and on validation cells only. The fix cannot keep its placeholder '[checked on … / not checked]'; the recorded fact is 'not checked'. In mechanics terms, 'modes above b can be amplified' is imprecise: a Chebyshev polynomial scaled to [a,b] stays below 1 in magnitude up to about a+b. The correct statement is that nonexpansion is no longer guaranteed. The caveat policy puts this caveat in 5.2, so it belongs here. Separately, Appendix D's 'holds for all evaluated cells' overclaims in the same way; that is outside this finding.

findings.quote: no certified error bound is provided (Appendix G.4), although the residual of Eq. (5) and a label-free lower bound on each cell's energy error (Appendix I) can be computed at run time
findings.problem: The 'although' clause suggests a run-time accuracy check exists. It does not: the energy error of Eq. (5) needs an interior solve with A for each direction, and the lower bound of Appendix I can flag a large error but cannot confirm a small one. With worst directions far above the sampled maximum, a user has no inexpensive way to certify a deployed cell.
findings.fix: Replace with: "no certified error bound is provided (Appendix G.4): the interior residual of Eq. (5) is available at run time, but the energy error it determines needs one interior solve per direction, and the label-free lower bound of Appendix I can detect a large error in a direction but cannot confirm a small one."
notes: defender(refuted): The current sentence is accurate and does not suggest a certificate. It first says plainly "no certified error bound is provided". It then names two quantities that really can be computed at run time. The interior residual r_I=(K û)_I takes one product, and Section 3.1 already says its A⁻¹-norm is the error measure, "available without the reference extension". The second is described as a "lower bound", which by definition cannot confirm a small error, and Appendix I says so explicitly ("a small value alone does not bound the error from above"). The fix drops the fact that the residual is computable and repeats Appendix I. The finding's premise that the worst directions lie "far above the sampled maximum" is not established anywhere in the paper; G.4 shows only that the sampled statistics give no bound on unsampled directions.

expert(modified): Confirmed. With 'although', the clause reads as if a run-time accuracy check existed. Eq. (5) needs r_I^T A^{-1} r_I, which is one interior solve per direction. Appendix I itself says that a small lower bound 'does not bound the error from above'. The proposed replacement is correct, but it drops the one true positive fact: the interior residual itself is available at run time. The introduction also relies on that fact ('provides a computable residual (Eq. (5)) rather than a certified bound'). The revision keeps it while saying plainly what it costs to turn the residual into an energy error.

findings.quote: We follow the second route with a learned, geometry-conditioned interior extension.
findings.problem: The introduction groups the method with static-condensation reduced-basis methods and inexact substructuring, then says only that it follows the second route 'with a learned extension'. Contribution (i) claims a construction principle whose variational part the same introduction calls classical. A referee asking what is new relative to inexact BDDC/FETI-DP (approximate extensions inside the energy, Ŝ ⪰ S) gets no single plain answer.
findings.fix: After "We follow the second route with a learned, geometry-conditioned interior extension." add: "Inexact substructuring uses the approximate extension only inside a preconditioner, so the outer iteration still converges to the exact solution; here the condensed stiffness formed from the learned extension is itself the model of the cell, its error remains in the assembled response, and the learned field is what keeps that error small at a fixed correction budget (Section 5.5)."
notes: defender(refuted): The fix adds novelty claims the paper does not make, mischaracterises the cited literature and repeats existing text. (1) Inexact BDDC/FETI-DP (Li & Widlund 2007; abstract checked in the local PDF) uses inexact subdomain solvers, such as multigrid, inside a preconditioner for the exact system. NICE's difference is that the approximate extension defines the operator itself (a Ritz model Ŝ=FᵀKF). Calling it "the same extension" and naming only the learned start and the training as new loses that difference. (2) "Training through the correction" as a novelty sits badly with Um et al. (2020), which the introduction itself cites as "networks trained through the solver". (3) The component reduced-basis sentence repeats paragraph 5 ("presuppose a common discrete space across the parameter family, which a cut removes"). The introduction already says what is new: paragraph 3 ("Unlike hybrid neural solvers ... the output is a condensed operator per cell that can be assembled, differentiated and improved"), paragraph 5 and contributions (i)–(iii). R3 judged the introduction clean apart from specific edits and asked to add no claims.

expert(modified): The gap is real. The introduction puts NICE on the same route as inexact BDDC/FETI-DP without saying how it differs, and a referee from domain decomposition will ask. The proposed contrast has two problems. First, it misses the essential mechanical difference. The cited abstracts (Dohrmann 2007; Klawonn & Rheinbach 2007) confirm that inexact substructuring approximates the solves only inside a preconditioner, while the Krylov iteration still runs on the original system and converges to the exact solution. In NICE the condensed stiffness is the model itself, so its error stays in the response, and this is why contribution (ii) exists. 'Multigrid cycles from a fixed start' is also imprecise. Second, the proposed sentence on component reduced-basis methods repeats paragraph 5 of the introduction, which already says they presuppose a common discrete space and an offline basis. The revision states the real distinction in one sentence, points to the Section 5.5 evidence, and leads into the next sentence ('The two kinds of error enter the structural response differently').

findings.quote: in every example a better initial field or a larger correction budget reduced the energy error
findings.problem: The 'better initial field' half is contradicted by the paper's own data. With 32 steps per stage, the zero interior start ends below the harmonic start on H2 and U2 under nodal forces (0.0056% vs 0.0246%; 1.19% vs 1.25%, Table ST08b). NICE ends above the corrected base network on M2, H2 and U2 (Table 3). Appendix D.1 itself notes that initial errors do not order corrected errors.
findings.fix: Replace "and in every example a better initial field or a larger correction budget reduced the energy error" with "and in every example a larger correction budget reduced the energy error".
notes: defender(modified): The problem is real. Table ST08b shows that at 32 steps per stage under nodal forces, the zero interior ends below the harmonic start on H2 (0.0056% against 0.0246%) and on U2 (1.19% against 1.25%). At 64 steps on H2 it is 1.09e-4 against 5.18e-4. Appendix D.1 notes that initial errors do not order corrected errors. The "larger correction budget" half holds: every row of ST08b decreases from 8 to 64 steps, as do the 5.5 sequences. The NICE versus corrected-base argument is weaker, because NICE's uncorrected field is not shown to be better, and per-configuration NICE versus corrected-base comparisons are excluded by decision 1. findings.section: 1. Introduction (first paragraph, 'Two approximations reduce this cost')
findings.quote: and of inexact substructuring [Dohrmann (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nla.514)
findings.problem: The sentence puts inexact substructuring (including Klawonn & Rheinbach 2007) with SCRBE as an approximation that 'alters only the interior response to each pattern', and the next sentences treat this as an interior error that enters the structural response. Inexact FETI-DP (and inexact BDDC) use approximate local and coarse solves only inside the preconditioner of a Krylov iteration on the saddle-point or original system. The iteration still converges to the exact discrete solution, so these methods leave no interior model error. The Klawonn & Rheinbach abstract says so: 'preconditioners ... allow for an inexact solution of the coarse problem', with 'convergence bounds of the same quality as for the standard FETI-DP methods'.
findings.fix: Replace "Approximating the interior extension on the complete retained space, the route of the static-condensation reduced basis element method [Huynh et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1051/m2an/2012022), [Ballani et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2017.09.014) and of inexact substructuring [Dohrmann (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nla.514), [Li & Widlund (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2006.03.011), [Klawonn & Rheinbach (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1758), alters only the interior response to each pattern." with: "Approximating the interior extension on the complete retained space, the route of the static-condensation reduced basis element method [Huynh et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1051/m2an/2012022), [Ballani et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2017.09.014), alters only the interior response to each pattern; inexact substructuring methods [Dohrmann (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nla.514), [Li & Widlund (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2006.03.011), [Klawonn & Rheinbach (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1758) also approximate subdomain and coarse solves, but only inside a preconditioner, so that their iteration converges to the exact discrete solution."
notes: defender(modified): The problem is real. The Dohrmann (2007) abstract says it approximates 'the direct solutions using preconditioners' inside the BDDC preconditioner. Li & Widlund replace the Dirichlet solvers by inexact ones or a trivial extension inside the preconditioner. The Klawonn & Rheinbach abstract covers inexact coarse and local Neumann solves inside a Krylov iteration on the FETI-DP saddle-point system, with 'convergence bounds of the same quality as for the standard FETI-DP methods'. In all three the iteration converges to the exact discrete solution, so grouping them with SCRBE ahead of 'The two kinds of error enter the structural response differently' is wrong. The fix needs one correction: 'also approximates the interior solves' is inaccurate for Klawonn & Rheinbach, who approximate the coarse problem and the local Neumann problems, not interior (Dirichlet) solves. The sentence that follows ('We follow the second route ...') still refers to the SCRBE route.

expert(modified): The problem is real. In Li & Widlund (2007, Sec. 7) the inexact solves (multigrid V-cycles for the subdomain Dirichlet problems and the partially subassembled coarse problem) enter only the preconditioner, and PCG solves the original discrete problem. The Klawonn & Rheinbach (2007) abstract (Crossref) says the inexact solves of the coarse problem and of the local Neumann problems sit in preconditioners for the FETI-DP saddle-point system, with convergence bounds as for standard FETI-DP. Dohrmann's approximate BDDC is likewise a preconditioner. None of these methods leaves an interior model error, so grouping them with SCRBE under 'alters only the interior response' and then discussing how 'an interior error' enters the response is wrong. The proposed rewrite is right in substance, but 'approximates the interior solves' does not fit Klawonn & Rheinbach, who approximate coarse and Neumann solves, not interior (Dirichlet) extensions. 'Subdomain and coarse solves' covers all three works and matches the wording proposed for Section 6.3.

findings.quote: Its lattice solve is an inexact substructuring iteration, with approximate interior extensions as in inexact BDDC and FETI-DP methods
findings.problem: In inexact BDDC (Li & Widlund 2007) and inexact FETI-DP (Klawonn & Rheinbach 2007), the approximate subdomain (Neumann/Dirichlet) and coarse solves enter only the preconditioner, and the iteration converges to the exact discrete solution. NICE instead runs preconditioned CG on the assembled learned operator (Section 5.8), so the approximation sits in the operator and leaves a model error. 'As in' presents the cited methods as doing the same thing. Also, Klawonn & Rheinbach approximate local Neumann problems and the coarse problem, not interior extensions.
findings.fix: Replace "Its lattice solve is an inexact substructuring iteration, with approximate interior extensions as in inexact BDDC and FETI-DP methods [Li & Widlund (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2006.03.011), [Klawonn & Rheinbach (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1758)." with: "Unlike inexact BDDC and FETI-DP methods [Li & Widlund (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2006.03.011), [Klawonn & Rheinbach (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1758), which use approximate subdomain and coarse solves only inside the preconditioner and therefore converge to the exact discrete solution, its lattice solve iterates on the assembled condensed stiffnesses \(\widehat S\) of the learned substructures, so that the approximation lies in the operator itself." Keep the following sentence ("Its output is a condensed operator per cell with a quantified and reducible error; whole-lattice iterative solvers are a different route (Section 6.4).") unchanged.
notes: defender(modified): The problem is real. Section 5.8 solves the lattices by PCG on the assembled learned matrix (the recomputed residual is taken against \widehat{\mathbb K}), so the approximation sits in the operator. In inexact BDDC (Li & Widlund) and inexact FETI-DP (Klawonn & Rheinbach) the approximate solves sit only in the preconditioner, so 'as in' is wrong. Klawonn & Rheinbach also approximate coarse and Neumann solves, not interior extensions. The fix has two flaws. 'Assembled learned operator' breaks the term map ('learned operator' becomes learned substructure or condensed stiffness). And its closing 'leaves the error quantified in Section 5.8' repeats the R3-prescribed sentence that follows ('Its output is a condensed operator per cell with a quantified and reducible error; whole-lattice iterative solvers are a different route (Section 6.4).'), which should stay as it is.

expert(modified): The problem is real, for the same reason as finding 3. Inexact BDDC and FETI-DP put the approximate subdomain and coarse solves in the preconditioner and converge to the exact discrete solution. Section 5.8 shows that NICE runs PCG with a K_PP-based two-level preconditioner on the assembled learned condensed stiffnesses, so its approximation sits in the operator. Klawonn & Rheinbach approximate Neumann and coarse problems, not interior extensions. The proposed replacement is correct but has two faults. (i) It uses 'learned operator', which the term map replaces with 'learned substructure' or 'condensed stiffness Ŝ'. (ii) 'leaves the error quantified in Section 5.8' repeats the R3-prescribed next sentence ('Its output is a condensed operator per cell with a quantified and reducible error; …'). A version phrased as a contrast avoids both and leads into the R3 sentence, which stays unchanged.

findings.quote: for multiscale finite elements [Hou & Wu (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcph.1997.5682)
findings.problem: The lower bound by the exact Schur complement holds only for conforming (Galerkin) multiscale bases. Hou & Wu (1997) also introduce the oversampling technique, which gives nonconforming basis functions, and for that variant the bound does not hold. As written, the sentence claims the property for multiscale finite elements in general, attributed to that paper.
findings.fix: Write "for conforming multiscale finite elements (without oversampling) [Hou & Wu (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jcph.1997.5682)".
notes: defender(refuted): The sentence makes a claim about one substructure: an admissible extension (J_P F = I, rigid-body or constant modes reproduced), evaluated in the energy form, gives a condensed stiffness that is bounded below by exact condensation onto the same retained DOFs (Ritz identity, Eq. (4); Appendix B). Oversampling does not break that. In Hou & Wu's oversampled MsFEM, the basis functions are combined so that psi_i(x_j) = delta_ij at the coarse vertices, they still reproduce constants, and each element stiffness is the energy a_K(psi_i, psi_j) of that element-level extension. So the element matrix still dominates the exact condensation onto the vertex DOFs. What oversampling breaks is global conformity: the assembled coarse problem stops being a Galerkin approximation and loses the global compliance bound. The sentence does not claim that global property. Narrowing it to 'conforming ... (without oversampling)' would restrict a correct statement and imply, wrongly, that the per-substructure Ritz bound fails for oversampled bases.

expert(confirmed): Correct in mechanics terms. A conforming MsFEM basis (local solves with boundary data prescribed on each coarse element) is an admissible extension of the coarse nodal values. Its Galerkin stiffness therefore bounds from above the exact Schur complement onto those nodes, which is the Ritz argument. Hou & Wu (1997) also introduce the oversampling technique against the resonance error. Oversampled bases are nonconforming across coarse-element boundaries, so their elementwise energy is not a Ritz upper bound and the property fails. The proposed qualifier '(without oversampling)' names the variant the claim covers and is short.

findings.section: 1. Introduction (paragraph on related energy-based and learned-solver work)
findings.quote: accelerate a global solve or learn solution maps; here the learned map is exactly linear in the retained displacement, so that its energy defines an assembled stiffness
findings.problem: The contrast rests on exact linearity, but one of the cited works, Boullé & Townsend (2023), learns an approximant to the Green's function. That is a linear solution operator, exactly linear in the forcing. What actually separates the present map is that it is a per-cell extension whose energy defines a condensed stiffness that can be assembled; linearity alone does not.
findings.fix: Rephrase to: "accelerate a global solve or learn solution maps of the whole problem; here the learned map is a per-cell extension, exactly linear in the retained displacement, so that its energy defines a condensed stiffness that can be assembled".
notes: defender(refuted): The current contrast is not linearity alone. It reads 'exactly linear in the retained displacement, so that its energy defines an assembled stiffness'. A map that is linear in a cell's retained displacement is a per-cell extension, and that is the distinction the fix wants. Boullé & Townsend (2023) learn the Green's function of the whole problem, a map that is linear in the forcing, not in a cell's retained displacement, and it has no energy that defines an assemblable stiffness. So the sentence is already correct and does not set the Green's-function work apart on the wrong ground. The fix rewords it and adds 'per-cell extension' and 'of the whole problem' without changing what it says.

expert(confirmed): Correct. Boullé & Townsend (2023) learn a Green's function, a solution operator that is exactly linear in the forcing, so linearity alone does not set the present map apart. Learned multigrid prolongations are also linear maps whose Galerkin product forms a coarse operator, but they serve a global solve, which the first clause already covers. What does set it apart is that it is a per-cell extension whose energy gives a condensed stiffness that can be assembled. The proposed rephrasing says this and stays consistent with the preceding paragraph ('a condensed operator per cell that can be assembled, differentiated and improved').

findings.quote: join oversampled bases by an overlapping partition of unity [Guo et al. (2026b)]
findings.problem: The description of PIML-OFEM leaves out one of its three main ingredients. After the condensed solve and fine-scale reconstruction, Guo et al. (2026b, Section 5 preamble and conclusions) start from the reconstructed displacement and run 'a small number of residual corrections on the original fine-scale equilibrium equations' (Jacobi-preconditioned CG). They use this step to improve strain, strain energy and topology-optimisation sensitivities, and they credit the accuracy of derived quantities to 'oversampled shape functions, overlapping compatibility mechanism, and small amount of residual correction' jointly. The intro presents the correction of a learned field as what sets NICE apart and lists only partition refinement, enrichment and oversampling as how this line of work controls error, so leaving this out misrepresents the closest competitor. Section 5.7 ('partition refinement, boundary enrichment or oversampling') and Supplementary Note S4 carry the same omission.
findings.fix: Replace "join oversampled bases by an overlapping partition of unity [Guo et al. (2026b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22019v1)" with "join oversampled bases by an overlapping partition of unity and correct the reconstructed fine-scale field by a few Jacobi-preconditioned conjugate-gradient iterations on the global equilibrium equations [Guo et al. (2026b)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.22019v1)". After "...at the price of tens of thousands of coarse degrees of freedom per cell." add: "Unlike the global residual correction that Guo et al. (2026b) apply after the condensed solve, the correction here acts at fixed retained displacement inside the extension that defines each cell's condensed stiffness, so it improves the assembled stiffness and not only the recovered field."
notes: defender(confirmed): Checked against arXiv 2607.22019 (scratchpad/2607.22019.txt). The Section 5 preamble says that 'after completing the condensed system solution and fine-scale displacement reconstruction, this paper uses the reconstructed displacement as the initial field and performs a small number of residual corrections on the original fine-scale equilibrium equations', using 'PCG ... with the diagonal terms of the global stiffness matrix as the Jacobi preconditioner'. The results section and the conclusions credit 'the oversampled shape functions, the overlapping compatibility mechanism, and a small amount of residual correction' jointly. This paper presents the deployment-time correction as what sets NICE apart, so leaving out the closest competitor's own correction step is a real misrepresentation. The fix describes Guo et al. accurately: a few Jacobi-PCG iterations on the global fine-scale equations, starting from the reconstructed field. Its contrast also matches NICE: the correction W acts at fixed retained displacement inside each cell's condensed stiffness, so it changes Ŝ, whereas Guo's correction changes only the recovered field. Nothing in the decisions or the caveat policy conflicts with it.

expert(modified): Confirmed against the local arXiv text 2607.22019. At the start of Section 5: 'after completing the condensed system solution and fine-scale displacement reconstruction… performs a small number of residual corrections on the original fine-scale equilibrium equations… PCG … with the diagonal terms of the global stiffness matrix as the Jacobi preconditioner'. It 'does not alter the previously constructed oversampled numerical basis functions or the overlapping finite element compatibility space'. The conclusions credit 'oversampled shape functions, the overlapping compatibility mechanism, and a small amount of residual correction' jointly. The current description leaves this out, although a correction is what NICE presents as its own contribution, so the finding stands. The proposed fix is right in substance. One wording should be tighter: the correction W does not act 'inside each cell's condensed operator'. It acts on the interior field inside the extension F = WÊ that defines Ŝ = FᵀKF. 'After the condensed solve' also matches the source more closely than 'after the solve'.

findings.quote: imposes rigid-body motion constraints and, in its self-consistent form, evaluates the stiffness
findings.problem: Huang et al. (2022) imposes only the consistency (partition-of-unity) relations of its Eq. (8): sum N_ixx = sum N_iyy = 1 and sum N_ixy = sum N_iyx = 0. These reproduce rigid-body translations only. The paper mentions no rotational constraint; it uses them to drop one node's outputs from the network. This manuscript treats reproduction of rigid-body motion, with the rigid-body kernel, as a defining structural property, so crediting full rigid-body constraints to Huang 2022 overstates that source. The N^TKN stiffness (its Eq. 9) is correctly attributed.
findings.fix: Rephrase to "imposes consistency constraints that reproduce rigid-body translations and, in its self-consistent form, evaluates the stiffness as \(N^TKN\)". If Huang et al. (2023) also imposes rotational modes (I could not verify this), write "imposes partition-of-unity [Huang et al. (2022)] or rigid-body-mode [Huang et al. (2023)] constraints" instead.
notes: defender(refuted): The clause describes the PIML line and cites Huang et al. (2022) and Huang et al. (2023) together. Huang et al. (2023, EML 63, 102041, Sect. 3.2; full text in scratchpad/guo/1-s2.0-S2352431623000871-main.txt, lines 790-800) says that 'the solution space of the FEA should contain the substructure's translational motion and rotate motion ... corresponding geometric constraints must be imposed on N_j^h and K~_j^h', and then imposes them. So 'imposes rigid-body motion constraints' is accurate for the cited line. The primary fix ('constraints that reproduce rigid-body translations') would understate the 2023 paper and introduce an error. The alternative split attribution is optional precision, not a correction: the current text is not wrong.

expert(refuted): The sentence describes the PIML line and cites Huang 2022 and Huang 2023 together. That pairing supports every clause. Huang et al. (2023, EML 63, 102041, Sec. 3.2) imposes translation constraints on N (Eq. 13) and rotation constraints (Eq. 14, written with the rotation matrix ω), and imposes the rigid-body kernel on K̃ (Eq. 15, K̃φ = 0 with six rigid-body modes). It also calls the N^TKN evaluation of Eq. (17) 'theoretically self-consistent', which is where the manuscript's phrase comes from. Huang 2022 contributes PIML itself, the consistency relations of its Eq. (8) and the N^TKN stiffness of its Eq. (9). The proposed main rephrasing ('consistency constraints that reproduce rigid-body translations') would understate the cited line, because Huang 2023 also imposes rotational modes. The fallback split is accurate but only adds citation clutter to an already dense sentence. No change is needed.

findings.quote: Coarse multiscale bases with fine-scale correction have been used in optimisation without scale separation
findings.problem: Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015, Sections 2.4.2 and 3) do not use a coarse multiscale model with a fine-scale correction. They state that MsFEM used as a solver gives sub-optimal designs with disconnected features. They therefore use the spectral MsFEM basis only as the coarse space of a two-level preconditioner (one symmetric Gauss–Seidel pre- and post-smoothing) for GMRES on the fully resolved system, converged to 1e-8. That places the work among the global-solve accelerators the same paragraph contrasts with NICE. The co-cited Efendiev et al. (2013, GMsFEM) is not an optimisation paper.
findings.fix: In the Introduction, replace "Coarse multiscale bases with fine-scale correction have been used in optimisation without scale separation [Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2015.02.028), [Efendiev et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2013.04.045)" with "Spectral multiscale coarse bases [Efendiev et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2013.04.045) have served in optimisation without scale separation as the coarse space of a two-level preconditioner for the fully resolved problem [Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2015.02.028)". Apply this together with finding 2, which replaces the following ", including … [Chen & Li (2026)](…)," clause. The rest of the sentence (Bonilla Moreno et al.) stays unchanged.
notes: defender(modified): The finding is substantially right. In Alexandersen & Lazarov (arXiv 1411.3923, Sect. 2.4.2) the spectral MsFEM basis is only the coarse solve of a multigrid-like preconditioner (one symmetric Gauss-Seidel pre- and post-smoothing) for GMRES on the fine-scale system. The fine system is converged to 1e-8 in Sect. 3 (1e-5 in the tolerance study), so the work belongs with the global-solve accelerators. A&L do cite GMsFEM [44] = Efendiev, Galvis & Hou (2013), so 'building on' holds. Two adjustments are needed. (1) A&L do not observe the sub-optimal designs themselves. They state conditionally that a coarse solver that is not accurate enough 'will result in sub-optimal designs', citing Lazarov (2014). So 'gave' overstates; 'can give' is accurate. (2) The replacement must end without the trailing comma, so that the Chen & Li clause (finding 2 changes it to '; in analysis, ...') joins cleanly.

expert(modified): The problem is real. Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015, Sec. 2.4.2) use the spectral MsFEM basis only as the coarse-grid solve of a multigrid-like preconditioner: one symmetric Gauss–Seidel pre- and post-smoothing, inside GMRES on the fine-scale system, converged to 1e-8 (Sec. 3). The proposed causal clause is misattributed, though. The statement that MsFEM used as a solver gives sub-optimal, disconnected designs is cited by A&L to Lazarov (2014, their ref. [18]). A&L's own reason, in Sec. 3, is cost: one accurate coarse solve needs a very large basis. Also, A&L cite GMsFEM (Efendiev et al. 2013, their [44]) only as a future offline strategy, and build on Galvis & Efendiev (2010) and Efendiev, Galvis & Wu (2011), so 'building on generalised multiscale finite elements' is loose. The revised fix drops the 'because' clause and cites GMsFEM for the spectral bases themselves. It replaces only the first clause and assumes finding 2's split of the Chen & Li clause. With both applied, the sentence reads: 'Spectral multiscale coarse bases [Efendiev et al. (2013)] have served in optimisation without scale separation as the coarse space of a two-level preconditioner for the fully resolved problem [Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015)]; in analysis, numerical shape functions on unfitted coarse elements have been conditioned against small cuts [Chen & Li (2026)], and for unfitted two-dimensional lattices BDDC has been combined with reduced-order cell stiffnesses [Bonilla Moreno et al. (2027)].' This also puts A&L with the global-solve accelerators named earlier in the paragraph.

Its full text (Computer-Aided Design 193, 104038) has no optimisation or design example: it covers conditioning of rMsFEM numerical shape functions on small cut coarse elements, convergence tests and a PCB thermal-conduction example. The words 'optimi…' appear only in its reference list.
findings.fix: Split the clause off the optimisation statement. Replace ", including numerical shape functions on unfitted coarse elements conditioned against small cuts [Chen & Li (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2026.104038)," with "; in analysis, numerical shape functions on unfitted coarse elements have been conditioned against small cuts [Chen & Li (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2026.104038),"
notes: defender(confirmed): Chen & Li (2026, CAD 193, 104038; full text in scratchpad/guo/1-s2.0-S0010448526000084-main.txt) is an analysis paper on conditioning rMsFEM numerical shape functions on unfitted reduced coarse elements. 'optimi' occurs only in its reference list. 'including' wrongly places it among optimisation uses. The replacement '; in analysis, ...' is correct and fits the revised clause of finding 1.

expert(confirmed): Confirmed from the full text of Chen & Li (Computer-Aided Design 193, 104038). The paper treats the conditioning of rMsFEM numerical shape functions on unfitted reduced coarse elements with small cuts. Its examples are linear elasticity and thermal conduction, including the large thermal PCB example of Sec. 5.6. It has no optimisation: 'optimi…' and 'design' appear only in its reference list. 'Including' therefore wrongly puts it among optimisation applications. The proposed split reads well whether or not the first clause is revised, and it works with the revised fix of finding 1 (the two replace disjoint text).

findings.quote: one convex separable approximation per analysis, solved by a primal–dual interior-point method, with no line search and no conservativeness test
findings.problem: The implementation described here and in Table ST21 is attributed only to Svanberg (1987). That covers the primal–dual interior-point subproblem solver, the a0/ai/ci/di problem form with elastic variables, the 0.5/1.2/0.7 asymptote rule and 'no conservativeness test (no GCMMA inner loop)'. The 1987 paper solves the subproblem by a dual method and has neither this problem form nor GCMMA. These come from Svanberg (2002, SIAM J. Optim.) and the 2007 KTH note, which the project's own mma.py names as its source for the problem form and the interior-point solver. Without that source, a0, ci and di in Table ST21 are undefined.
findings.fix: (a) Supplementary Note S9.1, first sentence: replace "The update is the standard method of moving asymptotes [Svanberg (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1620240207): one convex separable approximation per analysis, solved by a primal–dual interior-point method, with no line search and no conservativeness test (Table ST21)." with "The update is the method of moving asymptotes [Svanberg (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1620240207) in the form of Svanberg (2007): one convex separable approximation per analysis, solved by the primal–dual interior-point method of that note, with no line search and without the conservativeness test of its globally convergent variant GCMMA (Table ST21)." (b) Table ST21, row 'Optimiser': replace "\(a_0=1\), \(a_i=0\), \(c_i=1000\), \(d_i=1\)" with "constants of the problem form of Svanberg (2007): \(a_0=1\), \(a_i=0\), \(c_i=1000\), \(d_i=1\)". (c) Section 5.10: replace "takes one step of the method of moving asymptotes [Svanberg (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1620240207), with a move limit" with "takes one step of the method of moving asymptotes [Svanberg (1987)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1620240207) in the form of Svanberg (2007), with a move limit". (d) In the reference list, add directly after the Svanberg (1987) entry: "Svanberg, K. (2007). *MMA and GCMMA – two methods for nonlinear optimization*. Technical note, KTH Royal Institute of Technology, Stockholm."
notes: defender(confirmed): The implementation's own source (src_v2_wip/mma.py, header lines 3-9 and 65) names Svanberg (2007) as the source of the problem form (a0, a_i, c_i, d_i with elastic variables y_i, z) and of the primal-dual interior-point subsolver. ASYINIT/INCR/DECR = 0.5/1.2/0.7 are the 2007-note defaults. The 1987 paper has neither. Citing only Svanberg (1987) therefore leaves a0, c_i, d_i in Table ST21 without a source. Crossref confirms the 2002 entry: SIAM J. Optim. 12(2), 555-573, DOI 10.1137/S1052623499362822. The fix adds sources and keeps the 1987 citation, so no information is lost.

expert(modified): The problem is real. The project's mma.py names Svanberg (2007) as its source for the problem form (Eq. 1.1: f0 + a0 z + Σ(c_i y_i + d_i y_i²/2)) and for the primal–dual interior-point subproblem solver, and it uses the 0.5/1.2/0.7 asymptote rule. Svanberg (1987) solves the subproblem by a dual method, uses a different asymptote factor (s = 0.7, widened by 1/s) and has no a0/z term, so Table ST21's a0, a_i, c_i, d_i are undefined without the 2007 note. Crossref confirms the metadata of the 2002 paper (SIAM J. Optim. 12(2), 555–573). Two corrections to the proposed fix. (1) The supplement has no reference list of its own: latex/build_supp_tex.py says 'the supplement cites the main text', and every citation in the supplement is also cited in the main text. Adding references cited only in the supplement would leave entries in the main list that the main text never cites, which copyediting flags. The new reference should therefore also be cited where the main text names MMA (Section 5.10). (2) The 2007 note itself defines GCMMA, so one added reference is enough. The 2002 paper is not needed for a statement that GCMMA was not used. The fix also keeps the '(Table ST21)' pointer, which the proposed text dropped.

findings.quote: Approximating the interior extension on the complete retained space, the route of the static-condensation reduced basis element method
findings.problem: The sentence names inexact substructuring (Dohrmann 2007; Li & Widlund 2007; Klawonn & Rheinbach 2007) as an example of an approximation whose interior error then 'enter[s] the structural response'. In Li & Widlund the inexact interior solvers act only inside the preconditioner, so they change the convergence rate, not the solution. Unlike SCRBE and NICE, they leave no interior model error.
findings.fix: After the inexact-substructuring citations, qualify the clause: "… [Klawonn & Rheinbach (2007)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.1758), alters only the interior response to each pattern (in inexact substructuring only inside a preconditioner, so that the converged solution remains exact)."
notes: defender(confirmed): Li & Widlund (lw.txt, abstract and Sect. 3) build the inexact subdomain solvers into preconditioners for the original problem. Dohrmann (2007, 'An approximate BDDC preconditioner') and Klawonn & Rheinbach (inexact FETI-DP) do the same, so the converged solution stays exact. The next sentences ('The two kinds of error enter the structural response differently. An interior error is weighted ...') imply that the second route leaves an interior model error, which holds for SCRBE and NICE but not for inexact substructuring. The parenthetical qualification is accurate, short, and contradicts nothing.

expert(confirmed): Confirmed. In Li & Widlund (2007; NYU TR2005-871 text) the inexact subdomain solvers replace the exact Dirichlet and partially subassembled solves inside the BDDC preconditioner. The iteration runs on the fully assembled system, so inexactness affects only the convergence rate. The same holds for Dohrmann's (2007) approximate BDDC preconditioner and for the inexact FETI-DP methods of Klawonn & Rheinbach (2007). The next sentences ('The two kinds of error enter the structural response differently. An interior error is weighted by the energy …') would otherwise suggest that inexact substructuring leaves an interior model error in the response, which it does not. The parenthetical is accurate and short. 'Exact' here means the discrete solution, as elsewhere in the paper.

findings.quote: such as graded triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattices with supports, external loads and cells cut by the specimen boundary

Its abstract does not mention cells cut by the specimen boundary. Because the citation comes at the end of the whole noun phrase, it also appears to support the cut-cell feature, which is the paper's own motivation.
findings.fix: Move the citation so it supports only graded TPMS lattices: "Structures assembled from repeated thin-walled cells, such as graded triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) lattices [Yu et al. (2019)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.matdes.2019.108021) with supports, external loads and cells cut by the specimen boundary, call for a reusable component model of one cell."
notes: defender(confirmed): Yu et al. (2019, Mater. Des. 108021) are uniform and graded Schwarz P and Gyroid specimens made by stereolithography and tested in compression for energy absorption (Semantic Scholar abstract). The abstract has nothing on cells cut by the specimen boundary, which is this paper's own motivating feature. Moving the citation directly after 'graded ... (TPMS) lattices' keeps its support role, loses nothing, and the sentence still reads correctly.

expert(confirmed): Confirmed (Crossref and Semantic Scholar abstract). Yu, Sun & Bai (2019, Mater. Des. 182, 108021) is an experimental study: uniform and graded Schwarz P and Gyroid specimens made by stereolithography and tested in compression for energy absorption. findings.section: 5.7. Ablation: restricting the retained box-face representation
findings.quote: port-reduced methods control the resulting error by partition refinement, boundary enrichment or oversampling

Supplementary Note S4 (line 614) calls the same works (Huang 2024, Guo 2026a/b) 'reduced-boundary learned substructures'. expert(confirmed): Confirmed. The Introduction keeps 'port reduction' for Eftang & Patera (2013) and Smetana & Patera (2016), and calls the PIML line 'learned substructures described by a few boundary degrees of freedom'.
