findings.quote: and of relaxation after a learned initial guess [Zhang et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-024-00910-x)
findings.problem: HINTS (Zhang et al. 2024) is not relaxation after a learned initial guess. It interleaves relaxation sweeps with DeepONet steps that predict a correction from the current residual, at a fixed DeepONet-to-relaxation ratio (e.g. 1:24). The paper uses a one-time DeepONet initialiser followed by Jacobi only as baseline M2 (Fig. 2C), and reports that this initialiser's contribution 'is marginal – it does not change the convergence rate'. Attributing the learned-initial-guess-plus-relaxation pairing to this paper therefore misstates its method and the result it reports.
findings.fix: Replace the sentence with: "The pairing is that of smoothed-aggregation prolongation [Vaněk et al. (1996)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02238511) and of hybrid solvers in which relaxation removes the high-frequency error that a learned prediction leaves [Zhang et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1038/s42256-024-00910-x)."
notes: defender(modified): The problem is real. The local copy of HINTS (scratchpad/p/2208.13273.txt) describes M2, 'Jacobi solver initialized with a single DeepONet inference', as marginal: 'it does not change the convergence rate' (lines 164-170). HINTS itself interleaves DeepONet steps with relaxation (Algorithm, line 590: 'if kit mod nr = 0'). So 'relaxation after a learned initial guess' describes the baseline the paper rejects. The current sentence comes word for word from the R3 document, but it is a citation-accuracy matter, not one of the binding decisions 1-10. The proposed fix is accurate but has two drawbacks. It turns the sentence into a contrast that repeats the Introduction ('Unlike hybrid neural solvers, which combine learned predictions with relaxation ... [Zhang et al. (2024)]', M01 line 15). And its 'here it supplies the initial field once' invites comparison with the M2 result that HINTS calls marginal. A better fix keeps the 'pairing' wording the R3 document asked for and cites HINTS for what its abstract actually claims: networks miss high frequencies, relaxation resolves them. That point fits Section 4.2, which is about the error spectrum. 'Relaxation' is allowed under the term map when naming cited literature.

expert(confirmed): I checked arXiv:2208.13273v2, the HINTS paper. At a fixed ratio (1:24, 1:14) the authors alternate DeepONet iterations with Jacobi iterations, and the DeepONet takes the current residual r(x) as input and outputs the correction δv. Their baseline M2, 'Jacobi solver with DeepONet initializer, i.e., one-time usage of DeepONet followed by Jacobi iterations', is reported as 'marginal – it does not change the convergence rate'. So 'relaxation after a learned initial guess' attributes to Zhang et al. the very configuration they show to be ineffective. The sentence came from the R3 compression item [机械], which only shortened the text. It is not one of the author's binding decisions, so correcting the characterisation does not re-litigate anything. The fix is accurate. It uses 'relaxation' only to name the cited literature, which the term map allows, and it matches the Introduction's contrast with hybrid neural solvers.

findings.quote: [Ballani et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2017.09.014) and of inexact substructuring

Their method also reduces the retained (port) space, so it belongs to the first route, or to both. Huynh et al. (2013) by contrast states 'there is no reduction of the truth port degrees of freedom' and is correctly placed.

(2013)](https://doi.org/10.1051/m2an/2012022) and of inexact substructuring ...". Add it to the first list instead: "as in port reduction [Eftang & Patera (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1002/nme.4543), [Smetana & Patera (2016)](https://doi.org/10.1137/15m1009603), [Ballani et al. (2018)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2017.09.014) and in learned substructures ...". Alternatively, delete the citation here and remove the entry from the reference list, since it is cited nowhere else.

SCRBE port training is the empirical port reduction of Eftang & Patera (2013), so Ballani et al. reduce the retained (port) space. That contradicts 'alters only the interior response to each pattern'. Huynh et al. (2013) remains correctly placed. Ballani is cited only in this sentence in MANUSCRIPT_EN.md (reference entry at line 563), so moving it to the port-reduction list breaks no other reference and keeps the bibliography intact. Prefer the move to the delete alternative.

expert(confirmed): The Ballani et al. (2018) abstract (Semantic Scholar) says: 'We adapt the SCRBE port training procedures to anticipate the behavior of the field over the linear–nonlinear interface'. McBane et al. list [2] (Ballani) among the port-reduced static condensation works. So the method reduces the retained (port) space and does not fit only the 'complete retained space' route. findings.quote: treat isoparametric substructures [Zhang et al. (2026)]
findings.problem: The isoparametric PIML formulation was introduced by Zhang, Huang, Liu, Du, Cui and Guo (2024), Extreme Mech. Lett. 72, 102237 (2D). That paper is cited by the IJMS 2026 paper but not by this manuscript. The cited 2026 paper (title: 'Problem-independent transfer learning for complex-domain 3D topology optimization') contributes transfer learning from regular to isoparametric hexahedral substructures in 3D. [Problem-independent machine learning-enhanced structural topology optimization of complex design domains based on isoparametric elements](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eml.2024.102237). *Extreme Mechanics Letters*, 72, 102237." If the reference list cannot be extended in this round, use only "transfer them to complex three-dimensional design domains [Zhang et al. (2026)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ijmecsci.2026.112007)".
notes: defender(modified): The current text is not false: the 2026 IJMS paper does treat isoparametric substructures, and 'Isoparametric substructure' is one of its keywords. But its own abstract (scratchpad/guo/1-s2.0-S0020740326008611-main.txt) names its contribution as transferring representations 'learned from regular 3D substructures to complex isoparametric substructures'. The 2D isoparametric PIML formulation already exists in Zhang et al. (2024) EML 102237, which the 2026 paper cites (OpenAlex W4402665963 is in its reference list). Read in the list, 'treat isoparametric substructures [Zhang 2026]' implies the 2026 paper is the origin. The proposed 'extend them by transfer learning to ...' leaves 'them' without a clear referent in this list of variants. Use a list-parallel verb phrase that names the actual contribution. Adding EML 2024 is optional and adds a reference, so it is left to the author.

expert(modified): Crossref shows that the IJMS 2026 paper (Zhang, L., Liu, Guo, Jiang, Guo; 'Problem-independent transfer learning for complex-domain 3D topology optimization') cites 10.1016/j.eml.2024.102237. That earlier paper (Zhang, Huang, Liu, Du, Cui, Guo 2024, 'PIML-enhanced structural topology optimization of complex design domains based on isoparametric elements') is where the isoparametric PIML formulation appeared, and this manuscript does not cite it. Crediting 'isoparametric substructures' to the 2026 paper therefore misattributes it and omits the 2026 paper's own contribution, transfer learning to complex 3D domains. The proposed text adds a detail I could not verify: no abstract or full text of the 2026 paper is available (ScienceDirect blocked, Crossref and Semantic Scholar have no abstract). That detail is that the 2026 transfer is specifically to isoparametric hexahedral substructures. The revised text keeps only what the title supports and credits the isoparametric formulation to its origin.

findings.section: 1. Introduction (paragraph on related energy-based and multiscale models)
findings.quote: Coarse multiscale bases with fine-scale correction have been used in optimisation without scale separation
findings.problem: Efendiev et al. (2013, GMsFEM) is cited as an instance of coarse multiscale bases being used in optimisation, but the paper does not do any optimisation. It sets out an offline/online spectral enrichment of a coarse multiscale space for forward problems with parameterised inputs and has no fine-scale correction step. Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015) is the work that uses a spectral coarse basis in topology optimisation, and it cites GMsFEM only as a possible offline/online strategy, not as prior use in optimisation.
findings.fix: Cite Efendiev et al. only for the coarse basis and Alexandersen & Lazarov only for its use in optimisation: "Coarse multiscale bases [Efendiev et al. (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcp.2013.04.045) with fine-scale correction have been used in optimisation without scale separation [Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2015.02.028), including numerical shape functions on unfitted coarse elements conditioned against small cuts [...]" (delete the Efendiev link from its current position after Alexandersen & Lazarov).
notes: defender(confirmed): Efendiev, Galvis & Hou (2013) is the GMsFEM framework for forward problems: no optimisation and no fine-scale correction step. Alexandersen & Lazarov (2015) is the optimisation work: topology optimisation without length-scale separation, with a spectral coarse basis used as a preconditioner, which is the fine-scale correction (g2_al2015.txt abstract). Citing both after 'have been used in optimisation' attributes optimisation use to GMsFEM. The fix moves the Efendiev link to 'Coarse multiscale bases', removes no reference and keeps the sentence structure. Efendiev is cited only here (reference line 583).

expert(confirmed): In the local text of Alexandersen & Lazarov (arXiv:1411.3923), GMsFEM [44] is cited only as a possible strategy: 'an offline building of the basis for the possible variations of the design and using it in an online optimisation process [44]'. The authors then choose the other strategy. Efendiev et al. (2013) sets out a forward multiscale method and does no optimisation. A&L use the spectral MsFEM coarse basis as the coarse solve of a multigrid-like preconditioner with fine-scale smoothing, so 'with fine-scale correction ... in optimisation without scale separation' describes them correctly. The fix attaches each citation to the claim its paper supports and reads well.

findings.quote: adaptive FETI-DP coarse spaces [Heinlein et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1137/20M1344913)
findings.problem: The citation sits in a list of learned components that "accelerate a global solve or learn solution maps", but the descriptor leaves out what is learned. Adaptive FETI-DP coarse spaces are not themselves learned. In ML-FETI-DP (Heinlein et al. 2021), a neural network classifier predicts which local generalised eigenvalue problems can be skipped when the adaptive coarse space is built (up to 97% avoided), which cuts the setup cost. As written, a reader could think the network learns the coarse space.
findings.fix: Replace "adaptive FETI-DP coarse spaces [Heinlein et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1137/20M1344913)" with "machine-learning-assisted adaptive FETI-DP coarse spaces [Heinlein et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1137/20M1344913)".
notes: defender(modified): The problem is real but minor. Only the first list item carries the word 'Learned', and the coarse spaces in Heinlein et al. are not learned: a neural classifier decides where adaptive eigenvalue problems are needed (title: 'Combining machine learning and adaptive coarse spaces—a hybrid approach'). Of the two options offered, take the short one. It fixes the mischaracterisation without swelling a list that the R3 document already flagged as overloaded.

expert(confirmed): Crossref gives the title of 10.1137/20M1344913 as 'Combining Machine Learning and Adaptive Coarse Spaces—A Hybrid Approach for Robust FETI-DP Methods in Three Dimensions' (SISC 2021). The network is a classifier that decides which local generalised eigenvalue problems the adaptive coarse space needs. It does not learn the coarse space itself. Without that qualifier, the entry in a list of 'learned' solver components is misleading. Both proposed wordings are correct. The shorter 'machine-learning-assisted adaptive FETI-DP coarse spaces' fits the list's telegraphic style better.

findings.quote: Bendsøe, M. P., Sigmund, O. (2003). [*Topology Optimization: Theory, Methods, and Applications*]
findings.problem: The DOI 10.1007/978-3-662-05086-6 resolves to the second edition, which Springer lists with "Copyright: Springer-Verlag Berlin Heidelberg 2004" (edition number 2). Crossref gives issued = 2004 for this DOI. The year 2003 is a common citation convention but matches neither record, so a DOI-based reference check will flag the mismatch. The in-text citation in Section 3 ("[Bendsøe & Sigmund (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-05086-6)", part M03_sec3) carries the same year.

[*Topology Optimization: Theory, Methods, and Applications*](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-05086-6), 2nd edn. Springer, Berlin, Heidelberg.") and in the in-text citation in Section 3 ("[Bendsøe & Sigmund (2004)]"). Re-sort the reference list if needed.

Springer's book page lists several publication dates, the earliest in October 2002, for the print/eBook versions. The second-edition title page and the standard citation in CMAME and elsewhere use 2003. The verified bibliography (docs/paper_p1/references_verified.bib, key Bendsoe2003TopologyOptimization) gives year 2003 with the hardcover ISBN 978-3-540-42992-0. Changing to 2004 would make the entry inconsistent with that ISBN and the verified .bib. It would also require edits in M03 and in M11, and the brief marks M11 'not edited in this round'. The claim that a DOI-based check 'will flag the mismatch' is speculative: DOI matching resolves the record whatever the year. No change.

expert(confirmed): Crossref for 10.1007/978-3-662-05086-6 gives issued = published-print = 2004. The entry already says '2nd edn.', so the year should be that of the edition the DOI points to. The in-text citation sits in Section 3.2, Section 3, part M03_sec3, at line 107 of the joined MANUSCRIPT_EN.md, and needs the same change. The brief's note that M11_refs is not edited in this round described the R3 content pass, not an author decision, so a metadata correction does not conflict with any decision. Re-sorting is not needed, because the entry's position after Ballani and before later authors does not depend on the year.

findings.quote: Related energy-based models include embedded positive-semidefinite learned elements
findings.problem: Parish et al. (2024) do not learn an energy. They learn a displacement-to-force map f = K(u)u, where the learned stiffness K(u) is symmetric positive semidefinite and depends nonlinearly on the interface displacement (abstract and Section 1 of the paper). Their test cases involve finite deformation and contact, where such a map is not in general the gradient of a potential. Calling it an 'energy-based model' misdescribes this closely related work, which presents itself as a structure-preserving, learned static condensation of an embedded inner domain.
findings.fix: Replace with: "Related structure-preserving models include learned elements that condense an embedded inner domain into a symmetric positive semidefinite interface stiffness [Parish et al. (2024)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00466-024-02481-5) and convex neural energy elements, which ..." (rest of the sentence unchanged).
notes: defender(confirmed): Confirmed from parish2024.txt. The abstract says the model learns 'the map from displacements on the inner-outer domain interface boundary to forces', optionally 'by virtue of learning a symmetric positive semi-definite (SPSD) stiffness matrix'. Line 165 says 'we learn a mapping f = K(u)u'. The paper says 'our machine-learned surrogate performs static condensation of the inner domain degrees of freedom', and its tests involve finite deformation with contact. No energy is learned, so 'energy-based models' misdescribes it. 'Structure-preserving' matches the paper's own main line (L2), and the rest of the sentence, including the Jiang, H. et al. clause and the 'here one corrected extension ...' contrast, still reads correctly. The R3 item for this paragraph only split it into two paragraphs and does not fix this wording.

expert(confirmed): The local copy of Parish et al. (arXiv:2307.05434v3) is titled 'Embedded symmetric positive semi-definite machine-learned elements…'. It learns 'the map from displacements on the inner-outer domain interface boundary to forces', which in effect is a learned static condensation, with the SPSD-NN variant giving K_ML(u_h)u_h. It does not learn an energy, and its examples involve finite deformation and contact. Calling it 'energy-based' therefore misdescribes it, whereas 'convex neural energy elements' (Jiang, H. et al.) really are energy-based. The fix's 'structure-preserving' matches the paper's main line, and it adds the missing 'symmetric'. The rest of the sentence ('here one corrected extension defines both…') still follows.

findings.quote: for unfitted two-dimensional lattices BDDC has been combined with reduced-order cell stiffnesses
findings.problem: In Bonilla Moreno et al. the reduced-order model (MDEIM) only speeds up the assembly of each cell's full p-FEM stiffness matrix: it interpolates the trimmed-cell integrals. The local Schur complement is then formed exactly, and BDDC works on the full cell DOFs (abstract and Section 4 of arXiv:2604.09113v3). 'Reduced-order cell stiffnesses' can be read as reduced-dimension (condensed) cell models, which would make that work look closer to the present learned condensed stiffness than it is.
findings.fix: Replace "and for unfitted two-dimensional lattices BDDC has been combined with reduced-order cell stiffnesses [Bonilla Moreno et al. (2027)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2026.119304)" with "and for unfitted two-dimensional lattices BDDC has been combined with full cell stiffness matrices whose trimmed-cell integrals are approximated by a reduced-order model based on matrix discrete empirical interpolation [Bonilla Moreno et al. (2027)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cma.2026.119304)".
notes: defender(modified): Confirmed from bon_v3.txt (arXiv:2604.09113v3). The abstract says 'To accelerate the assembly of the cell stiffness matrices, we combine a fast assembly technique ... with a reduced order model (ROM) based on the matrix discrete empirical interpolation method (MDEIM)'. Line 637 says 'the local Schur complements are assembled explicitly'. So the ROM approximates trimmed-domain integrals for assembly and does not produce reduced-dimension cell models, and 'reduced-order cell stiffnesses' can be misread. The proposed fix is accurate but heavy for an introduction list. A shorter wording that follows their abstract is clearer.

expert(modified): The local copy of arXiv:2604.09113v3 confirms the finding. The ROM (MDEIM) only speeds up assembly of the trimmed-cell integrand tensor, after which 'the local Schur complement S(i) is then formed' explicitly on the full cell DOFs. 'Reduced-order cell stiffnesses' therefore suggests condensed, reduced-dimension cell models, which they are not. The proposed text is accurate, but the parenthetical 'reduced-order (matrix discrete empirical interpolation) model' is awkward, so I tightened it.

findings.quote: recover linear fields by exact interior lifting
findings.problem: 'Linear fields' is unclear and can be read as linearly varying (affine) fields. In Jiang, H. et al. (2026), interior fields are recovered by the exact lifting U_i = -K_ii^{-1} K_ib U_b, which needs the tile mesh, assembly and one factorisation and back-solve per element. The authors themselves say this removes the speed advantage for full fields (Section 4, 'What is accelerated, and what is recovered'). That per-element exact solve is the point of the contrast with NICE's single corrected extension, but the current wording hides it.
findings.fix: Replace "and recover linear fields by exact interior lifting [Jiang, H. et al. Claims-to-evidence map, summarised. Every number in the abstract and conclusions matches the body:
- 0.074% mean energy error: Section 5.3
- 0.28% / 1.5% two-cell maxima: Section 5.6, Table ST09b (0.27% / 1.49%)
- 81–110 s against 868–1,042 s: Table 5
- 0.0051 design difference: case A, Table 6
- 43 min for 110 cells: Table ST26
- 27–37% homogenised underestimate: Table ST23c
- below 0.04% / 0.33% on the plates: Table ST27
- 787–932 s saving and the pay-back estimate: Table 5 and Section 5.1
- 0.02–0.13% / 0.22–0.35% gradient errors: Table ST19 only

Promises kept:
- The outline (Sections 2–7) is kept.
- The three contributions are each delivered:
  - (i): Section 4.1, Eq. (4), Appendices B and E, Section 5.2.
  - (ii): Eqs. (7) and (9), Appendices C.1 and H.1, Sections 5.6 and 5.8.
  - (iii): Sections 5.1–5.10.
- The openings of Sections 2–4 match what those sections do.

Remaining problems, in four groups:
1. Missing hypothesis. Improvability at deployment is asserted without its containment hypothesis in the Introduction's thesis sentence, contribution (i), Section 2.3 and Section 4.1. Section 4.3, Section 6.2 and the conclusions do state it. Contribution (i) also drops the condition A ≻ 0 that Sections 2 and 6.4 keep.
2. Causal attribution the paper does not support. The amplification ε = δ²κ is credited to 'thin walls' in the Introduction, Section 2 and the conclusions. The measurements tie it to the cuts: the uncut U2 has κ = 85 and ε = 0.40%. Appendix B.3 explicitly declines a mechanical interpretation.
3. Selective or ambiguous statements in the conclusions and abstract:
   - 'hardest cell' is undefined.
   - 'better initial field' has counterexamples in ST08b.
   - 'one to four orders' should be 7–12,000×.
   - The single-case design reproduction is stated as general.
   - The homogenised model is contrasted on compliance error while its designs come within 1.1% (and are better in bending).
   - 'transfers to other families' is untested.
4. Underclaims for the main line:
   - The deployment-only correction of the base network across the population (6.89% → 0.0965%) is missing from the abstract.
   - The linear sensitivity term is shown only where it is negligible; Table ST05a shows it at 28–72% in the smaller-error cells.
   - The near-sharpness of the share-weighted bound in the lattices is not announced.
   - The ablation result is absent from the conclusions.

Smaller pointer and source issues: the Introduction's 'coarse DOFs' conflicts with the meaning in Sections 4.3 and 5.5; the 37–50% cut-band share has no table; Section 6.2 cites Sections 5.8 and 5.9 for numbers that appear only in Table ST19; the ε = δ²κ pointer should be Appendix B.3; the requirement lists in the Introduction and Section 2.3 do not match.

No front-matter number contradicts the body. The 0.3% in the conclusions versus 0.28% in the abstract is a precision inconsistency only.

I wrote down 20 questions a CMAME referee would ask and looked for where the main text answers each. The main pattern: the evidence for the hardest questions usually exists, but it sits in the supplement or in project records, while the main text answers defensively, twice, or not at all.

Answered adequately in the main text:
- **Port reduction:** introduction paragraphs 2 and 4, the 5.7 ablation, and 6.1.
- **Common discrete space for reduced-basis interiors:** introduction paragraph 5.
- **Offline cost and pay-back:** 6.3 gives about 60 GPU-hours, recovered after a few hundred design iterations, roughly ten case-A optimisations; the arithmetic checks out (216,000 s / 787–932 s ≈ 230–275 iterations).
- **Trained parameter domain and orientation dependence:** 5.10 and 6.4.
- **Discrete switches in design:** 3.3, 5.10 and 6.2.
- **Field-based versus complete derivative:** 3.3, 6.2 and 6.4.
- **Selection versus held-out cells:** 5.1, 5.6 and Table ST09b.
- **One seed:** 6.4.

Questions that are unanswered, weak, or contradicted by data in the paper or the project records:
- **(1) Worst-case versus sampled directions.** Only the sampled maximum (1.24%) appears in the main text, and ε_* is defined but never reported. A search on 16 validation cells finds NICE directions of at least 44.5% and 8.8% (median 0.23%; followup/A/full16/SUMMARY.md). The wording "maximum of 1.24%", "a finite direction set samples" and the 6.4 "although … can be computed at run time" together leave the reader thinking the operator error is bounded near 1%.
- **(2) Fair hardware baseline.** Table 6 itself shows exact condensation on the GPU at 469 s against 141 s for NICE, about 3.3×, while the abstract, 5.9 and 7 quote about 10× against CPU direct solution. The main text never discusses this or says why the direct routes run on the CPU.
- **(3) Attribution of the 1.31 factor.** It mixes training through the correction with a 15,000-step continuation on a larger set. The matched control (Uncorrected continuation plus W) is not reported, and Table 3 reverses the factor on 3 of 5 cells.
- **(4) What training through W buys versus a larger deployment budget.** Base network with 16/Q1/16 beats NICE on every Table 3 cell (ST08b). NICE itself is never shown to improve with a larger budget, although the conclusions claim improvability at deployment and overstate the "better initial field" ordering.
- **(5) Learned versus harmonic start at equal cost.** The network-pass cost is not reported.
- **(6) Outside the training family.** 6.4 says "not tested", but a gyroid zero-shot test exists (draft S10: 4.5% mean, 25.6% largest, 13.5% lattice sensitivity).
- **(7) Scaling with the number of cells.** Stated only in S9.6 (about 23 s per cell); no baseline beyond eight cells.
- **(8) Variant designation on the 80 validation geometries.** Stated only in Table ST01.
- **(9) Spectrum containment on deployment cells.** Verified only on the validation set.
- **(10) Whole-lattice AMG/BDDC.** Defensive in 6.3 and repeated in 6.4.
- **(11) Novelty relative to inexact BDDC/FETI-DP.** Not stated plainly.
- **(12) Minor items:** CMS/Craig–Bampton is never named; linearity and stresses are out of scope but unstated; the 3% threshold is not explained; the n = 32 caveat does not say what it implies; the discrete-reference caveat is repeated four times; 6.1 re-reports the 5.3/5.5 numbers; "coarse degrees of freedom" in the introduction is ambiguous; 591 versus at most 153 geometries visited.

Recommended priority: the three high findings (worst-direction disclosure, the GPU exact twin, the 1.31 attribution). Each changes how a referee reads a headline number.

Most uses are accurate. Xu 1992 as the subspace-correction and energy-projection framework is fine. So are Falgout et al. for the two-grid error operator, Adams et al. for polynomial smoothing and Pfaff et al. as a mesh-based graph network. Guo 2026a is described correctly as Bézier boundary enrichment, and the S4 detail '56 control points per substructure' matches their Sec. 2.3: 8 vertex, 24 edge and 24 face control points, 168 DOFs.

The one serious problem is the Introduction sentence on Guo et al. (2026a, Table 1). It cites only the 10×10×10 case, gives error growth as the reason the full-node option was set aside, and leaves out that this option was the most accurate at 5×5×5 (0.84%) and was dropped mainly for cost. The project's own GUO_SERIES_COMPARISON_CN.md also records cost as the reason. The two inexact FETI-DP/BDDC passages describe preconditioner-only approximations as if they were operator approximations. The caveat policy keeps the Guo numbers in the Introduction, so the proposed fix stays there.
